assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made a superconducting circuit a controllable quantum-optical system: strong coupling of a qubit to a single microwave photon in a resonator, dispersive readout and the architecture now underlying most superconducting processors. The idea is original, clean and has had large downstream impact on quantum information, microwave quantum optics and quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Blais and collaborators (with Schoelkopf's group at Yale) proposed the architecture in 2004 and Wallraff et al. gave the first strong-coupling demonstration, with Schoelkopf's group developing the readout, transmon and many follow-ons. A three-person split is defensible, but Girvin and Huang are not in the supplied credit, and the relative roles of proposal versus experiment are disputed in emphasis. I disclose that this is my own subfield and Chalmers/WACQT are close to it.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: reproduced by dozens of independent groups for two decades, with multi-qubit processors and error-correction experiments built on it. Timing is a judgment call because the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits; this is a distinct, later discovery, but the committee may want some distance.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to follow the 2025 circuit prize so soon with a related one.
Credit division between the original theoretical proposal, the first experiment and the transmon/readout developments; Girvin and others are not available in the credited names.
My own proximity to the field requires a conflict disclosure and discounting of enthusiasm.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal showed how a string of trapped ions could implement quantum logic gates, and ion experiments then realised high-fidelity gates, entanglement of many qubits and small algorithms. It is a founding architecture for quantum computing with a clear, specific discovery and wide impact.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive theoretical proposal; Blatt's group provided leading experimental realisations (Innsbruck). Wineland, already recognised in 2012 for ion control, and Monroe, Wineland and others are not in the credit, which complicates fairness and the experimental half of the prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature: gates, entanglement and commercial ion processors have been demonstrated by several independent groups for roughly two decades. Recognition is timely, with a long, well-established record.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize to Wineland and with candidate B044 and B038, which share Cirac and Zoller.
Experimental credit beyond Blatt (for example Monroe, Wineland) is not in the supplied names.
Scalability of ion machines compared with other platforms is still open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials as a field, with highly tunable strong correlations in a single clean platform. The originality and breadth of impact are exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery. This is a fair three-person configuration, though other groups (Dean, Yacoby, Young, and Cao as first author) contributed important parallel confirmation and extensions, and these names are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Fast-maturing: the key results are widely reproduced, but the field is only about eight years old and the superconducting mechanism and many correlated phases are not settled. Recognition may be slightly premature.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of several correlated phases are unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate interpretation.
Relatively recent compared with usual Nobel timescales.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators established a new class of band topology, with protected edge and surface states, and shaped much of modern condensed-matter physics. It is conceptually original and widely influential, building on the 2016 topological-phase prize.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the foundational 2005 theory; Molenkamp's group gave the HgTe experimental demonstration of the edge states after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. Zhang is deceased and the BHZ proposal sits outside the credit, and Hasan's 3D observation is excluded by the three-name limit. Credit allocation is therefore delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent confirmations in HgTe, Bi-based compounds and many later materials over almost two decades; recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: The BHZ prediction and Zhang's death make a fully fair attribution difficult.
Practical applications remain limited, although scientific impact is large.
Partial overlap with the alternative candidate B025.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and developed by Ye into clocks at the 10^-18 level, transformed time-keeping and enabled tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The discovery is original, clear and of lasting precision-measurement impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive magic-wavelength lattice proposal and early realisation; Ye drove the extension to record accuracy and stability. A two-person configuration is clean Other strontium and ytterbium clock groups also contributed, and Ye's comb work built on the 2005 prize area.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent clocks in several laboratories reach comparable accuracy, and redefinition of the second is under discussion. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Other clock groups (ytterbium, ion clocks) may share relevant credit.
Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
The redefinition of the SI second has not happened yet.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes, together with fault-tolerant ideas, made large-scale quantum computing conceivable by showing that noise can be handled with finite overhead. The idea is original and extremely consequential for quantum technology and, through the surface and toric codes, for topological physics.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane introduced the first quantum codes in 1995-96 and Kitaev introduced topological codes and fault-tolerant ideas. Calderbank, Gottesman, Aharonov, Ben-Or, Knill and Laflamme are not credited, so the fairness of a three-person split is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Theory is mature, but experimental confirmation is recent: logical-qubit improvement and below-threshold surface-code operation have been shown in the last few years, mainly in superconducting circuits and also in atoms and ions. As a prize for a physics discovery this is somewhat early, and it is in my own area of interest.
uncertainties: The experimental demonstration of useful, scalable error correction is still emerging.
Many contributors besides the three credited (Gottesman, Calderbank, Knill, Aharonov and others).
Whether this is physics or computer science, and my own stake in quantum-computing programmes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with exquisite control (Mott insulator transition, single-site microscopy), opening quantum simulation of many-body physics. The experiments are original and have broadly influenced condensed-matter and AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) made the Hubbard-model proposal; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott-insulator observation and quantum-gas microscopy. The proposal side is shared with Cirac and Jaksch, and the Hubbard-lattice experiments also involved Hansch and Esslinger, which limits clean three-person attribution.
assessment.maturity: Mature in technique with many independent groups, but the promise of quantum simulation solving open many-body problems is only partly realised. Timing is reasonable but not urgent given earlier BEC and cooling prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap in Cirac and Zoller credit with other candidates.
Esslinger, Hansch, Jaksch and others also contributed significantly.
Quantum-simulation advantage over classical methods is not yet decisively demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned the no-cloning and entanglement properties of quantum mechanics into a proposed secure-communication protocol (BB84 and E91), with a strong conceptual foundation and growing practical use. It follows the 2022 prize on entanglement tests, and has clear conceptual importance.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 and Ekert E91; the three form a natural theory trio. Pan's experimental satellite and network demonstrations are widely cited but he would be a fourth name, and the list restricts me to three, so I am proposing the theory trio only.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are mature and have been implemented in multiple independent experiments; practical security and device loopholes keep evolving. Recognition would be timely, though part of the physics already shares the 2022 prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement and quantum information science.
Experimental credit for Pan and others lies outside a three-theory-person configuration.
Practical security loopholes and implementation maturity remain debated.
